issues.legal_issue: The authority empowered to appoint a manager to conduct a business may also terminate that manager’s appointment.
material_facts: The appellant was appointed as manager of two businesses vested in the Custodian of Evacuee Property under statutory management powers.
The Deputy Custodian later terminated the appellant’s management and required him to hand over possession.
issues.conclusion: The management could lawfully be terminated by the Deputy Custodian; the appointment power carried an implied power to suspend or dismiss the appointee.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(b) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, read with section 16 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, gives the appointing authority power to suspend or dismiss a person appointed under that power, unless a different intention appears. The termination power is an incident of the appointment power.

predicates.manager_appointed_under_management_autho: A public authority appointed a person to manage a business under its authority to appoint managers for that purpose.
predicates.termination_order_made_by_competent_cust: An authority competent to make the appointment ordered that the manager’s appointment be terminated.

issues.definition: When a public authority appoints a manager under its management authority and a competent authority orders termination, the appointment may be terminated by that authority.

issues.legal_issue: An otherwise competent public officer’s order is not invalid merely because it refers to the wrong source of authority or describes the officer by another official title.
material_facts: The order terminating the appellant’s management was signed by an officer who described himself by a title associated with another statutory role.
The order was within the officer’s competence under an authority that remained in force, and the officer also held the relevant Deputy Custodian role.
issues.conclusion: The termination order was valid despite its description as an order under another role, because the officer had competence to make it under the authority that remained in force.
issues.legal_principle: An order within an officer’s competence is judged by its substance rather than its form and may be attributed to an existing authority under which it is valid, even if it purports to rely on another source of power. The Court relied on Balakotaiah v. The Union of India, [1958] S.C.R. 1052.

predicates.order_within_officers_competence: The officer who made the order had legal competence to make that order under an available authority.
predicates.alternative_authority_remained_in_force: A source of authority under which the officer could validly act remained in force when the order was made.
predicates.order_referred_to_different_official_rol: The order described the officer or its source of power by reference to a different official role.

issues.definition: If an officer was competent under an authority that remained in force, referring to a different official role does not by itself invalidate the order.

issues.legal_issue: Mandamus is unavailable to enforce an obligation arising only from a contractual appointment rather than a statutory duty.
material_facts: The appellant sought writ relief challenging the termination of his management and seeking restoration of possession.
The appointment as manager was contractual in nature, and no statutory obligation between the appellant and the public officer was identified.
The Court considered this point even on the assumption that the termination order was illegal.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the termination was illegal, the appellant could not obtain mandamus to enforce obligations arising from the contractual appointment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, mandamus compels performance of public duties prescribed by statute; it does not enforce an obligation arising only from a contract. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay Presidency and Aden v. Bombay Trust Corporation Ltd., 63 I.A. 408, and P. K. Banerjee v. L. J. Simonds, A.I.R. 1947 Cal. 307.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_mandamus: The applicant brought a proceeding seeking mandamus against a public officer.
predicates.appointment_obligation_is_contractual: The obligation relied on by the applicant arose from a contractual appointment.
predicates.no_statutory_duty_owed_to_applicant: No statutory duty requiring the officer to perform the requested act was owed to the applicant.

issues.definition: When an applicant seeks mandamus to enforce a contractual appointment obligation and the officer owes no corresponding statutory duty, mandamus is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A preliminary decision to allot property does not create a final allotment or a concluded contract when the terms remain unsettled.
material_facts: The appellant’s appointment as manager was expressly temporary, pending any outright allotment.
Government communications stated that allotment had been decided in principle, that the terms would be communicated later, and that the appellant would meanwhile continue as manager.
The terms and conditions were never finally settled, and the appellant sought possession of the businesses through writ proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The communications did not make a final allotment or establish a concluded contract of sale, so the appellant had no legal right to the businesses on that basis and was not entitled to mandamus for possession.
issues.legal_principle: A decision in principle, with terms and conditions left for later determination, does not establish a concluded contract of sale or a final allotment. Article 226 does not provide mandamus to enforce a right that has not been established. No earlier case was relied on for this point.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_writ_for_possession: The applicant sought writ relief to obtain possession of property on the basis of an alleged allotment.
predicates.allotment_terms_remain_unsettled: The terms and conditions of the proposed allotment had not been finally settled.
predicates.communications_are_preliminary: The communications described the proposed allotment as a decision in principle and deferred its terms to a later determination.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks possession by writ on the basis of preliminary allotment communications whose terms remain unsettled, no final allotment or concluded sale contract exists.
